source: AP Classroom, AP Physics 1 (course 92), Videos tab, units 1-8. Read 2026-11-09. EK alignment is Claude's best guess from each video's description; review before relying on it.
videos: In this video, we will differentiate scalars and vectors by looking at some examples. We'll also look at why it's useful to call some directions "positive" and others "negative."
In this video, we will add vectors in one dimension.
In this video, we will analyze the motion of multiple objects along vertical and horizontal number lines to demonstrate displacement, as well as select convenient coordinate systems for measurement.
In this video, we will define average velocity, use speed data to calculate acceleration, and practice answering conceptual questions about acceleration and velocity.
In this video, we will describe motion using equations for position and velocity as functions of time. We'll also develop an idea of what a "rate of change" means.
In this video, we will use a ticker tape to represent motion as a number line, a position vs. time graph, a velocity vs. time graph, and kinematic equations.
In this video, we will use kinematic equations and velocity vs. time graphs to solve for unknown values in motion problems.
In this video, we will analyze the special case of free fall near the surface of a planet or moon. We'll also calculate the launch speed of a projectile based on its time in the air.
In this video, we will create position, velocity, and acceleration vs. time graphs from an object's motion, and show how the graphs describe that motion.
In this video, we will describe motion when acceleration and initial velocity are in opposite directions.
In this video, we will define "frame of reference" and discuss how to pick a convenient one.
In this video, we will describe the position and velocity of an object from the point of view of observers in different reference frames.
In this video, we will discuss how to add right-angle vectors and demonstrate graphical and analytical methods of vector addition using a pirate treasure map.
In this video, we will use trigonometry to break vector quantities into useful parts called components. We'll also practice adding those components.
In this video, we will analyze the motion of an object moving as a horizontal projectile and discuss the independent horizontal and vertical motions of that object.
In this video, we will analyze projectile motion with equations and graphs, and discuss important points in an object's projectile motion.
In this video, we will describe what center of mass is and how it can be used to describe changes to objects or systems.
In this video, we will calculate the location of the center of mass of several systems of objects and then check our results experimentally.
In this video, we will show experimentally how the center of mass of a system obeys Newton's laws.
In this video, we will describe the forces exerted on an object using a free-body diagram.
In this video, we will examine the force exerted when two objects press against each other, which is called a normal force.
In this video, we will describe the rules for drawing free-body diagrams for forces at an angle, including on an object sliding up and down an incline with friction.
In this video, we will describe the interaction between two objects using Newton's third law.
In this video, we will explore Newton's third law and consider how it explains the forces exerted by two interacting objects.
In this video, we will draw free-body diagrams for objects in equilibrium, communicating the object exerting and experiencing each force.
In this video, we will discuss how to break forces into components for an object on an incline.
In this video, we will identify what factors affect the acceleration of a system.
In this video, we will discuss how the direction of a force relates -- or doesn't relate -- to the direction of motion.
In this video, we will apply Newton's second law to situations inside of an elevator.
In this video, we will apply Newton's second law to systems of objects, like an Atwood machine.
In this video, we will make qualitative and quantitative predictions about the tension in the string in a modified Atwood machine and then measure that tension.
In this video, we will define the gravitational field strength, g, and discuss what determines its value at various locations.
In this video, we will use the law of universal gravitation to determine the strength of the gravitational force between two bodies.
In this video, we will predict changes to the gravitational force when density, size, or mass of an object changes.
In this video, we will use free-body diagrams to explain apparent weightlessness on zero-gravity flights and in space stations.
In this video, we will distinguish between gravitational and inertial mass.
In this video, we will define friction and discuss the difference between static and kinetic friction.
In this video, we will determine what factors affect the magnitude of friction between two surfaces.
In this video, we will experimentally determine the coefficient of kinetic friction on an incline.
In this video, we will discuss multiple experimental methods of measuring a spring constant.
In this video, we will investigate experimentally whether a rubber band obeys the same force vs. distance relationship as does an ideal spring.
In this video, we will draw free-body diagrams for objects moving in circular paths and determine what causes the acceleration of the objects.
In this video, we will discuss how forces acting perpendicular or parallel to displacement affect the motion of an object.
In this video, we will describe the relationships between net force, speed, mass, and radius in circular motion.
In this video, we will make semi-quantitative predictions about circular orbits.
In this video, we will derive Kepler's third law and investigate the relationships it predicts.
In this video, we will define translational kinetic energy and describe how it is affected by speed.
In this video, we will define work and describe how to calculate this new quantity.
In this video, we will perform an experiment to determine how work done by a force depends on the angle of the force.
In this video, we will explore how work done on a system will change the kinetic energy of a system.
In this video, we will define elastic potential energy and show how it can be calculated using a graph.
In this video, we will define gravitational potential energy and emphasize the importance of measuring changes in this quantity near Earth's surface.
In this video, we will learn why it is necessary to define a new equation for gravitational potential energy that can be applied to any system.
In this video, we will look at ways to use energy bar charts to represent energy transformations depending on the defined system.
In this video, we will use a conservation of energy equation to discover how different variables affect each other.
In this video, we will solve for unknown quantities and derive equations using conservation of energy.
In this video, we will justify a predicted outcome based on conservation of energy.
In this video, we will define power and how it changes with work done.
In this video, we will develop an experimental procedure to determine power use and explore how changes to mass and time affect power use.
In this video, we will define momentum and look at some examples of calculating momentum.
In this video, we will define impulse by looking at a cart changing momentum.
In this video, we will look at another definition of impulse by calculating the area under a force vs. time graph.
In this video, we will see how the impulse-momentum relationship is equivalent to Newton's second law and how it can be used to make predictions and solve problems.
In this video, we will learn how to define a system, how to calculate the total momentum of a system, and how to determine the center-of-mass velocity of a system.
In this video, we will derive the conservation of momentum equation both mathematically and using experimental results.
In this video, we will practice translating between different representations for collisions.
In this video, we will translate between representations and examine what happens when we analyze a system in which momentum is not conserved.
In this video, we will define the types of collisions and how to determine which type of collision being analyzed.
In this video, we will design an experiment, and analyze different collisions to determine which type of collision they would be.
In this video, we will define a rigid system and describe its angular displacement in radians. We'll also define average angular velocity and acceleration.
In this video, we will make graphs to find relationships between angular displacement, velocity, and acceleration.
In this video, we will use previously made graphs to derive a symbolic expression for rotational kinematics.
In this video, we will compare the motion of two spinning objects using graphs of their motion.
In this video, we will relate linear distance traveled to angular displacement.
In this video, we will use equations to relate linear velocity and tangential acceleration to angular velocity and angular acceleration, respectively.
In this video, we will quantitatively compare linear and angular quantities within a rigid system.
In this video, we will define torque and qualitatively compare the torques applied on a rigid body.
In this video, we will learn the difference between force diagrams and free-body diagrams.
In this video, we will quantitatively compare the torques exerted on an object.
In this video, we will define rotational inertia and determine the rotational inertia of a system of objects about an axis.
In this video, we will qualitatively determine the rotational inertia of various rigid bodies.
In this video, we will compare the rotational inertia of a rigid body when it rotates about its center of mass to when it rotates about any other axis.
In this video, we will explore the conditions that cause a system to be in rotational equilibrium.
In this video, we will show how to mathematically describe a system in rotational equilibrium by finding the net torque.
In this video, we will discuss the applications of Newton's first and second laws for rotating systems.
In this video, we will explore the relationship between applying a net torque to a system and how the system's angular velocity changes.
In this video, we will conduct an experiment to help us understand the relationships between angular acceleration, torque, and rotational inertia.
In this video, we will practice using Newton's second law in rotational form to analyze an Atwood's machine with a massive pulley.
In this video, we will practice using Newton's second law in rotational form to analyze a modified Atwood's machine with a massive pulley.
In this video, we will compare rotational and translational kinetic energies, as well as derive the relationship for rotational kinetic energy for a rigid body.
In this video, we will investigate the relationships among rotational kinetic energy, rotational inertia, and angular velocity.
In this video, we will derive the work done by a torque and relate it to our previous studies of work and kinetic energy.
In this video, we will discuss an experiment designed to investigate the relationship between work done by a torque and the work and kinetic energy involved.
In this video, we will discuss ways to determine the angular momentum of an object or a rigid system.
In this video, we will describe the angular impulse delivered to an object or rigid system by a torque.
In this video, we will relate an object's or rigid system's change in angular momentum to the angular impulse given to that object or rigid system.
In this video, we will describe the total angular momentum of a system.
In this video, we will describe the behavior of a system using conservation of angular momentum.
In this video, we will describe how the selection of a system determines whether the angular momentum of that system changes.
In this video, we will describe the kinetic energy of a rolling, rigid body.
In this video, we will describe the motion of a rigid body that is rotating without slipping, and relate the translational and rotational quantities for that body.
In this video, we will look at examples of systems that are rolling with and without slipping.
In this video, we will examine the motion of satellites in circular orbits.
In this video, we will examine the motion of satellites in elliptical orbits and compare the motion to circular orbits.
In this video, we will further define the gravitational potential energy of a satellite and a massive central object and use this idea to calculate escape velocity.
In this video, we will define simple harmonic motion and the restoring force.
In this video, we will define the period of a pendulum and the period of spring. We'll also use a simulation to determine how changing variables will affect the period.
In this video, we will design a procedure to analyze the period of a pendulum and determine an experimental value of g.
In this video, we will show how a specific equation models the motion of an object-spring system, and investigate the physical parameters represented by each variable in this equation.
In this video, we will provide evidence that a bowling ball pendulum displaced by a small angle can be modeled as a simple harmonic oscillator.
In this video, we will consider and experimentally verify the positions at which the displacement, velocity, and acceleration of a simple harmonic oscillator are at their extremes.
In this video, we will investigate energy transformations during oscillatory motion using graphs and other representations.
In this video, we will use conservation of energy to describe simple harmonic motion (SHM).
In this video, we will analyze oscillatory motion and practice our reasoning skills using conservation of energy, conservation of momentum, and other laws of physics.
In this video, we will review the three main states of matter, as well as determine the density of an unknown liquid by graphing the mass of the liquid versus its volume.
In this video, we will introduce the concept of pressure as force per unit area and use it to calculate the weight of a car using a tire pressure gauge and a meterstick.
In this video, we will compare gauge pressure and absolute pressure, as well as experimentally determine the factors that affect the absolute pressure of a liquid.
In this video, we will investigate the factors that do and do not affect the buoyant force acting on an object interacting with a fluid.
In this video, we will derive the equation for the buoyant force based on the difference in pressure between the top and bottom of an object submerged in a fluid.
In this video, we will determine how the density of an object affects how much of the object is submerged in a fluid.
In this video, we will apply the law of conservation of mass to derive a symbolic expression for the speed of a fluid in a tube through a varying cross-sectional area.
In this video, we will apply the continuity equation to compare the speed of an incompressible fluid at various locations in a tube of varying cross-sectional area.
In this video, we will experimentally apply the law of conservation of energy to determine how the speed and vertical position of a fluid in a tube affect its pressure.
In this video, we will apply both the continuity equation and Bernoulli's equation to calculate the pressure of a fluid in a tube of varying cross-sectional area and height.
In this video, we will look at a special case of Bernoulli's equation, Torricelli's theorem, and how it relates to the speed of a fluid exiting an opening.
